📊 Graph Analytics
Top 15 Most Connected Symbols
Symbols with the highest combined in + out degree are the load-bearing pillars of your codebase.
A very long bar on an internal helper is a red flag — it means many things depend on one place that wasn't designed as an API.
Node Distribution by Kind
Shows what your codebase is made of at a glance — heavy on functions vs. classes vs. types.
A dominant slice (e.g. 80% variables) can indicate over-abstraction or, conversely, too little structure.
Degree Distribution — Connectivity Curve
Healthy codebases show a steep left peak (most symbols have few connections) and a long tail.
A flat or multi-modal curve signals coupling problems — too many symbols are over-connected.
Top 15 Callers — Highest Out-Degree
High out-degree means this symbol knows too much about the rest of the system — a classic god-object signal.
If the top callers are entry points or orchestrators that's fine; if they're utility helpers, consider splitting them.
Top 15 Callees — Highest In-Degree
These are your real public API — change them and many things break. High in-degree is expected for core utilities.
Surprise entries here (a private helper, a constant) indicate hidden coupling you should make explicit.
Files by Symbol Count
Files with many symbols are candidates for splitting — they likely handle multiple responsibilities.
Cross-reference with the coupling matrix: a large file that also couples to many directories is a high-priority refactor target.
Edge Kind Distribution
Tells you which relationship patterns dominate: calls, imports, inheritance, containment.
An unusually high import ratio vs. calls can mean modules are tightly wired at the file level without using each other's symbols.
Dead Code by Kind
These symbols are never referenced from within the indexed codebase — strong deletion candidates.
Focus on functions and classes; variables and constants are more likely to be used via dynamic patterns not captured by static analysis.
Symbol Count per Directory
A single directory holding most symbols is a monolith smell — the rest of the structure may be cosmetic.
Balanced distribution suggests good separation of concerns; a very tall single bar suggests your folder structure doesn't reflect your actual architecture.
Exported vs Unexported by Kind
Shows how much of each symbol type is intentionally public. A large unexported slice is healthy — it means most logic is encapsulated.
If nearly everything is exported, your module boundaries are weak and consumers have too much surface area to depend on.
Directory Coupling Matrix
Each row is a source directory, each column is a target — a bright cell means many edges cross from that row's folder into that column's folder.
Symmetrically bright off-diagonal pairs (A↔B and B↔A) reveal circular coupling between modules that should be cleanly layered.
In-Degree vs Out-Degree Scatter
Top-left = Sinks (referenced a lot, calls nothing) — typical for pure data types or leaf utilities.
Bottom-right = Sources (calls a lot, rarely referenced) — often entry points or wiring code. Top-right = Hubs — investigate these first.
Average Degree per File
Files with high average degree are deeply entangled regardless of their size — even a 2-symbol file can score high.
This metric catches hidden complexity better than raw symbol count: a small file with a huge average is often the real coupling hotspot.
